Feature card Rich Text 1:
BEROAS (Break-Even Return On Ad Spend) is the minimum ROAS you need to hit so you don't lose money on your ad campaigns. Below it, every sale costs you money. Above it, you start turning a profit.

Unlike a "magic" ROAS pulled from some YouTube tutorial, your BEROAS is personalized. It factors in your real costs: product, shipping, transaction fees, fulfillment.

Dropshipping example

You source a product at 39 € all-in (purchase, shipping, Stripe fees). You resell it for 89 €. Net margin: 50 €.

BEROAS = 89 ÷ 50 = 1.78x

You need to generate at least 1.78 € in revenue for every euro spent on ads to break even.
Feature card Rich Text 2:
Compare your BEROAS to your current ROAS. Three scenarios, three clear actions.

ROAS < BEROAS: you're losing money on every sale. Cut the campaign or rework your offer (price, upsell, sourcing cost).

ROAS = BEROAS: you're breaking even. Acceptable on retargeting, risky on cold traffic. Optimize before scaling.

ROAS > BEROAS: you're profitable. Scale in steps of 20% per week max so you don't break the algorithm.

Example: BEROAS at 3.5x, ROAS at 3.2x. Verdict: you're losing 8% on every sale without even realizing it.
Rich text area:
The BEROAS formula

Two formulas to know depending on what you want to calculate.

Simplified formula

BEROAS = 1 ÷ Net profit margin

Detailed formula

BEROAS = Selling price ÷ (Selling price − Total cost)

Total cost = COGS + shipping fees + transaction fees

COGS (Cost Of Goods Sold) covers the product purchase from your supplier or agent. Transaction fees include Stripe, PayPal, or your payment processor (usually 2.5 to 3%). Don't forget packaging and fulfillment cost if you go through a warehouse.

Worked example

Selling price: 89 €. COGS: 22 €. Shipping: 14 €. Stripe fees: 3 €. Total cost: 39 €.

BEROAS = 89 ÷ (89 − 39) = 89 ÷ 50 = 1.78x

BECPA, your handy complement

BECPA (Break-Even Cost Per Acquisition) gives you the maximum acquisition cost you can afford per sale, in euros.

BECPA = Selling price − Total cost = Gross margin

In the example: BECPA = 50 €. You can spend up to 50 € in ads per sale to break even. Handy when you think in CPA rather than ratio.

How to improve your BEROAS?

Four concrete levers to push your BEROAS up without changing products.

Lower your sourcing cost

Negotiate with your supplier as soon as you pass 50 orders a day. Ask for a volume discount, a better unit price, or switch to an agent who'll find you the same factory 20 to 30% cheaper. Compare 3 to 5 suppliers on Alibaba before you commit.

Raise your selling price

Margin is won as much on the sell side as on the buy side. Work on your positioning, add bundles (buy 2, get 1 free), offer a premium version 30% more expensive. A well-placed upsell raises your average order value by 15 to 40% without touching your acquisition cost.

Optimize your transaction fees

On Shopify, move to the Advanced plan once you pass 50k € in monthly revenue. You cut your transaction fees from 2% to 0.5%. On Stripe, negotiate your rate starting at 100k € in annual volume. Sounds small, but on 1M € in revenue you get 15,000 € net back per year.

Find products with a better ratio

The fastest lever is to start with a product that has a better margin from day one. Look for products with a high perceived selling price and a low sourcing cost. Copyfy lets you analyze the winning products of the moment and see directly which ones drive the best margins among your competitors.

Feature card Rich Text 2:
Your profit margin is the percentage of revenue left after every cost is paid. Not just the product - shipping, transaction fees, ad spend, returns, all of it.

The formula:

(Revenue − Total Costs) / Revenue × 100 = Profit Margin %

Example: you sell a product for €50. Your total costs (product + shipping + fees + CPA) are €35. That's a 30% net margin - solid.

Why does it matter before launch? Because a product that looks profitable at a glance can bleed money once you factor in a €12 CPA and a 2.9% payment fee. Run the numbers first. Always.
Feature heading 2: What counts as a good margin?
Rich text area:
What is a good profit margin for dropshipping?

There's no single answer - it depends on your price point and how efficiently you run ads. But here are the benchmarks most experienced dropshippers use:

  • Impulse buy (under €30): target net margin of 40–60%.
  • Mid-ticket (€30–€100): target net margin of 25–40%.
  • High-ticket (over €100): target net margin of 15–25%.

20%+ net margin is the widely cited healthy threshold. Below 10%, you're one bad ad week away from losing money.

BEROAS as a complementary metric. Margin % tells you profitability per order. BEROAS tells you the minimum your ad campaigns must perform to stay in the green. Use both - they answer different questions.

These are benchmarks, not rules. A store with a 15% margin but a highly optimized ad account can outperform one with 35% margin and a bloated CPA. Ad spend efficiency changes everything.

Gross margin vs. net margin: what's the difference?

Dropshippers often confuse the two. Here's the short version:

Gross margin - what it includes: revenue minus product cost and shipping. What it ignores: ad spend, platform fees, and returns. Typical dropshipping range: 30–60%. Use it for: evaluating supplier pricing.

Net margin - what it includes: revenue minus ALL costs (product, shipping, ads, fees, returns). What it ignores: nothing - it's the real number. Typical dropshipping range: 10–25%. Use it for: evaluating actual profitability.

Gross margin is useful for product selection. Net margin is what you actually take home. This dropshipping profit margin calculator gives you the net margin - the one that counts.

How to improve your dropshipping margin

Margins are squeezed from both sides: costs go up, ad performance goes down. Here's where to push back:

Source better. Negotiate with your supplier or switch to a cheaper one. A €2 reduction in product cost on 200 orders/month is €400 straight to your bottom line.

Pick higher-margin products. A product with a 3× markup beats a 1.5× markup every time, assuming similar demand. Use a dropshipping calculator before you commit to a product - not after.

Cut your CPA. Better creatives, tighter audiences, smarter bidding. Your CPA is the most volatile cost in the equation - and the one you have the most control over.

Increase your AOV. Add upsells, bundles, or a free-shipping threshold. More revenue per order with the same fixed costs = better margin.

Kill unnecessary fees. Payment processors, apps, platform fees - audit them quarterly. Small leaks sink ships.

How to use the tool

How detection works

We load the homepage and one product page, and look for the footprint each app leaves in the code (scripts, tags, CSS classes). If an app runs on the visitor side, it leaves a trace, and we read it.

What it detects

Apps with a visible footprint: reviews (Judge.me, Loox, Yotpo, Okendo…), upsell and cross-sell (ReConvert, Vitals, AfterSell…), email and SMS (Klaviyo, Omnisend, Postscript…), page builders (PageFly, GemPages, Shogun…), currencies, loyalty, subscriptions, popups, search, bundles.

The limits

Back-office-only apps (accounting, logistics, suppliers) leave no trace on the visitor side: invisible to any detector, including a Chrome extension. A store behind an aggressive firewall can also block the scan.

Feature Tilte 1: What is the real cost of a Shopify subscription?
Feature card Rich Text 1: The price on Shopify's pricing page is only part of the bill. On top of the subscription come a commission on every sale you collect, $0.30 fixed per order, and extra transaction fees if you collect somewhere other than Shopify Payments. The real cost of a plan depends on your volume, not on its sticker price.
Feature card Rich Text 2: A plan that costs more per month carries a lower commission rate. So there is a precise revenue figure at which the commission saving beats the extra subscription: that is your switching point. Below it you pay for nothing. Above it you leave money on the table with every order.
Feature heading 2: When should you change Shopify plan?
Rich text area:
How it works

  1. Your monthly revenue and order count, typed into the first two fields.
  2. Your billing mode and your payment processing mode, in one click.
  3. The total cost of every plan, the cheapest one highlighted, and your switching point.

What the calculation covers

  • The subscription, at the monthly or the annualised rate
  • Your plan's card rate, plus the $0.30 fixed fee taken on every order
  • The share of your sales paid with Amex or other premium cards, which is charged more
  • Third-party transaction fees, if you do not collect with Shopify Payments
  • The budget you spend on apps and side subscriptions

Shopify pricing at a glance

The four plans, with the subscription price and the commissions charged on each order. The annualised rate is the yearly payment brought back to a monthly figure.

PlanMonthlyAnnualisedStandard cardExternal gateway
Basic$39$292.9% + $0.302%
Grow$105$792.7% + $0.301%
Advanced$399$2992.5% + $0.300.6%
Plusfrom $2,300not sold yearlynegotiated0.2%

The Plus plan is not sold on a yearly rate and does not publish its card rates, which are negotiated case by case. The calculator reuses the Advanced rates, so the cost shown for Plus is a ceiling, never an underestimate.

Why the cheapest plan is not the cheapest

A Basic subscription costs $50 less per month than Grow on annual billing, but its card rate is 0.2 points higher. At $25,000 in monthly revenue the two are even. Above that, every dollar collected widens the gap in favour of Grow. The same logic separates Grow and Advanced, much higher up.

That is exactly what the switching point under the comparison computes: the revenue at which the plan above becomes worth it, at a constant average order value.

Shopify Payments or an external gateway

Leaving Shopify Payments costs twice: your new provider's rate, plus the third-party transaction fee Shopify charges in return. That fee falls as the plan goes up, which sometimes flips the ranking.

  • Basic: 2% third-party transaction fee
  • Grow: 1%
  • Advanced: 0.6%
  • Plus: 0.2%

When you pick the external gateway mode, the calculator also shows what the same volume would cost with Shopify Payments. On many stores, the gap pays for several months of subscription.

What this calculation leaves out

The rates used are the US price list in dollars, excluding tax. International cards add 1% on top of the rates shown. Left out: the specific commissions of certain payment methods, the cost of your domain name and any outside services. The goal is to compare plans on what actually separates them.

What the Shopify product exporter gives you

Every field below is filled from what the storefront publishes, one column per Shopify import column.

  • Product title, handle and full HTML description
  • Vendor, product type and the complete tag list
  • Every variant with its options, in the store's own option names

Why the file imports straight into Shopify

Most exporters hand you a spreadsheet that you then have to reshape by hand. This one writes the import format itself, which removes the whole remapping step.

  • The 42 official columns, in Shopify's order, so the importer recognises every one of them
  • One row per variant, with the option names repeated exactly as the importer expects
  • Products with more images than variants get extra rows carrying only the handle, the image URL, its position and its alt
  • A UTF-8 byte order mark, so accented titles open correctly in Excel and Google Sheets instead of turning into mojibake
  • Inventory tracking left empty on purpose, so imported products are sellable straight away instead of landing as sold out

Images are carried by URL. Shopify downloads them from the source store during the import, so you do not have to move any file yourself.

Who uses it, and what for

Reading a competitor's catalogue in full

Browsing a store shows you a few dozen products. The export shows you all of them at once, with prices, variant depth and the exact wording of every description. Sorting by price or by variant count surfaces the range structure in seconds.

Product research backed by real store data

A catalogue is a list of bets, not a list of winners. Cross it with the spy on competitor ads to see which of those products carry actual ad spend, and for how long. That is the difference between a product a store sells and a product a store sells well.

Migrating or duplicating a store

Moving your own catalogue to a second store, a test theme or a new market means exporting on one side and importing on the other. Since the file already matches the import format, the round trip is two operations.

Auditing a catalogue in bulk

Opened in a spreadsheet, the export makes gaps obvious: products with no meta description, images with no alt text, variants with no SKU, compare-at prices left over from an old sale. Filtering on an empty column is faster than clicking through the admin.

What the tool cannot export, and why

A storefront publishes what it needs to display products. Everything that lives only in the admin stays out of reach, for every store including yours.

Tool Feature Section Paragraph: What this calculator tells you about your customers
Feature card Rich Text 1: Customer lifetime value, or CLV, is the total margin a customer leaves behind between their first order and the day they stop coming back. It rests on three things: how much they spend per order, how often they order in a year, and how many years they stay. As long as you only look at the first sale, you underestimate the customer and cap your acquisition budget far below what you could afford.
Feature card Rich Text 2: Your maximum acquisition cost comes from lifetime value, not from your ad budget. The benchmark is a 3:1 ratio between what a customer brings in and what they cost to win: below it you stop covering fixed costs, and above 5:1 you are handing market share to competitors willing to pay more than you.
Feature heading 2: How much can you pay to acquire a customer?
Rich text area:
What is customer lifetime value (CLV)?

Customer lifetime value is the total profit you can expect from one customer over the whole time they keep buying from you. Not one order. Every order that customer will ever place, minus what it costs you to serve them.

That single number changes how you run a store, for three reasons.

  • It sets the maximum you can pay to acquire a customer, which is the only thing that makes an advertising budget rational instead of superstitious
  • It measures profitability across the relationship instead of per transaction, so a first order sold near break-even stops looking like a mistake
  • It shows which customers deserve retention spend, and the gap between your best and worst cohorts is usually wider than the gap between your best and worst products

Most stores never calculate it, then wonder how a competitor outbids them on every keyword and still makes money. That competitor is not luckier. They know the second order exists and they price acquisition against it.

CLV vs LTV: is there a difference?

No. CLV means customer lifetime value, LTV means lifetime value, and the two are used interchangeably in e-commerce and in SaaS. Anyone who tells you one is strictly per customer and the other per account is describing a convention, not a rule.

The distinction that does matter is revenue CLV versus margin CLV. The same customer can be worth 600 EUR of revenue and 270 EUR of margin. Since your acquisition cost is paid in real money, only the margin version can be compared with it. This calculator works on margin, which is why it asks for your gross margin instead of just your revenue.

What CLV is not

Three numbers get mistaken for lifetime value, and each one leads to a different bad decision.

  • Average order value measures one transaction. A store can have an excellent average order value and a terrible lifetime value if nobody comes back
  • Repeat purchase rate tells you how many customers order again, not how much profit that represents. Twenty percent of customers reordering a 12 EUR refill is not the same business as ten percent reordering a 200 EUR kit
  • Total revenue per customer ignores what the orders cost you. It is the version that makes an unprofitable store look like a growth story

Lifetime value is the only one of the four that can be compared with an acquisition cost, which is the whole reason to calculate it.

Why CLV matters for dropshippers and e-commerce stores

Dropshipping runs on thin margins and rising acquisition costs. A store that only breaks even on the first order has no room left: one bad week of ad performance and the whole thing is underwater. The stores that survive are the ones where the second and third order exist, because that is where the margin lives.

Take two stores with the same 40 EUR acquisition cost and the same 35 EUR margin per order. The first sells a decorative item bought once: lifetime value 35 EUR, a 0.9:1 ratio, dead on arrival. The second sells a consumable reordered three times a year for two years: lifetime value around 200 EUR, a 5:1 ratio, and enough room to outbid the first store on every single ad auction.

Same margin per order. Same acquisition cost. Opposite outcomes, decided by the product catalogue before a single ad was written.

How to calculate customer lifetime value: the formula

Simple CLV formula

The standard customer lifetime value calculation multiplies four variables:

CLV = average order value × purchase frequency per year × customer lifespan in years × gross margin

With a 100 EUR average order value, 4 orders a year, a 3 year lifespan and a 20% gross margin, CLV is 240 EUR. That is the profit one customer leaves behind across the relationship, and the ceiling for everything you spend to win them.

Average order value is total revenue divided by the number of orders. It is the easiest variable to move in the short term and the one most stores neglect.

Purchase frequency is how many times the average customer buys in a year. It is decided mostly by what you sell: a coffee brand is reordered monthly, a suitcase brand every five years.

Customer lifespan is how long a customer keeps buying before going quiet. It comes from your churn: lifespan = 1 / annual churn rate. If 30% of customers never come back within a year, lifespan is 1 / 0.30, so 3.3 years.

Gross margin is what stays after the cost of goods, shipping and payment fees. If you are not sure of yours, run it through the dropshipping profit margin calculator first, then come back here with a clean number.

This calculator asks for your retention rate rather than a lifespan in years, because retention is something you can pull out of your own order history, while a lifespan in years is usually a guess. It converts it for you with 1 / (1 - retention), which is the same arithmetic seen from the other side.

Predictive CLV formula (advanced)

The formula above treats every customer as the average customer. Predictive CLV does not. It uses probabilistic models, typically BG/NBD for how often someone buys and a Gamma-Gamma model for how much they spend, to estimate a value per customer from their individual transaction history. The reference work is Fader and Hardie's research on probability models for customer base analysis, and it is what large retailers run in production.

It is more accurate, and it costs more. You need clean order-level data, a pipeline that refreshes it, and someone who can read the output. For a store doing a few hundred orders a month, the simple formula gets you within range of the truth and the decision it drives, how much you can pay for a customer, is identical. Move to predictive CLV when segment-level precision starts changing your budget allocation, not before.

CLV formula in Excel or Google Sheets

To run the calculation across your whole customer base rather than on an average, build a five column sheet and let the sixth column do the maths.

ColumnContentExample
ACustomer ID1042
BAverage order value100
CPurchase frequency per year4
DLifespan in years3
EGross margin0.20
FCLV formula=B2*C2*D2*E2

Export your customers from Shopify, fill columns B to E, drag the formula down and sort by CLV. The interesting part is not the average that comes out, it is the shape of the distribution: on most stores the top 20% of customers carry more than half the profit, which tells you exactly who your retention budget belongs to.

Four mistakes that break a CLV calculation

The formula is simple enough that most errors come from the inputs, not the maths.

  • Using revenue instead of margin. The most common one, and it inflates the answer by whatever your cost of goods is. It turns a 2:1 business into a 5:1 fantasy
  • Guessing the lifespan. Three years sounds reasonable and is usually optimistic. Derive it from churn instead: 1 divided by the share of customers who do not come back
  • Using an all-time average. A store that changed its product mix or doubled its prices last year is averaging two different businesses. Use the last twelve months
  • Forgetting the cost of keeping the customer. Support, returns, loyalty discounts and platform fees are paid every year the relationship lasts, and on low margin catalogues they eat a surprising share of the lifetime value

Get those four right and a back of the envelope calculation is accurate enough to set an acquisition budget. Get them wrong and no amount of modelling sophistication will save the answer.

How to use this CLV calculator (step by step)

Step 1: enter your average order value (AOV)

The average amount a customer spends in a single purchase. Divide total revenue by total orders over the same period, or read it in Shopify under Analytics, then Reports, in the sales reports. Fifty thousand euros of revenue across 500 orders gives a 100 EUR average order value. Use a full quarter so a single promotion does not distort it.

Step 2: enter your purchase frequency

How many orders the average customer places in a year. Divide orders by unique customers over twelve months: 200 orders from 100 customers is a frequency of 2. Shopify shows the raw material for it under Analytics, Reports, customer behaviour, next to your repeat purchase rate. If you launched recently, use what you have and be conservative rather than hopeful.

Step 3: enter your gross margin

The percentage left after the cost of goods sold, shipping and payment fees. A product that costs you 20 EUR and sells for 50 EUR carries a 60% margin. This is the field that turns a flattering revenue number into a figure you can actually compare with your acquisition cost.

Step 4: enter your annual retention rate

The share of customers who are still buying a year later. Take the customers who bought more than twelve months ago and count how many ordered again since: that ratio is your retention. On a dropshipping or single-product store it is usually in the single digits, and 5% to 10% coming back is already decent. Established brands with a real catalogue, consumables or subscriptions reach 20%, 40% and beyond. The calculator turns it into an average lifespan with 1 / (1 - retention), so 40% retention means 1.7 years.

Optional: acquisition cost, service costs and discount rate

Adding your customer acquisition cost unlocks the CLV:CAC ratio, the payback period and the maximum CAC you can afford. Service costs cover support, returns and loyalty programmes, paid every year the customer stays. The discount rate brings future margin back to today's value; leave it at zero unless you are building a financial model.

Reading your results: CLV, annual value and CLV:CAC ratio

The headline figure is your customer lifetime value in margin. Under it sits the annual customer value, the margin one customer produces in a single year, which is the number your cash flow actually sees.

Then come the ratios. Net CLV is what remains once acquisition is paid for. The CLV:CAC ratio compares value to cost and drives the badge: critical below 1:1, low between 1:1 and 3:1, healthy between 3:1 and 5:1, and above 5:1 you are under-investing in acquisition. Payback tells you how many months it takes to earn your acquisition cost back, and the retention strip at the bottom shows what your customer would be worth at 20%, 40% or 70% retention, so you can see the value of a retention point before you spend anything to gain it.

A worked example, start to finish

Take a skincare store. Average order value 68 EUR, customers order 2.4 times a year, gross margin 45%, annual retention 40%, and support plus returns cost about 6 EUR per customer per year. Acquisition currently costs 32 EUR.

Annual margin per customer is 68 x 2.4 x 0.45, minus 6, so 67 EUR. Retention of 40% gives a lifespan of 1.7 years, which puts lifetime value at roughly 112 EUR and net value at 80 EUR once acquisition is paid. The ratio lands at 3.5:1, healthy, with payback in about six months.

Now change one variable. Retention at 60% instead of 40% takes the lifespan to 2.5 years and lifetime value to about 168 EUR, a 3.4:1 ratio at a much higher acquisition cost: this store could pay 50 EUR per customer instead of 32 and still be in the safe zone. That is 18 EUR more per customer to outbid competitors with, bought entirely with retention work rather than ad budget.

What is a good CLV for an e-commerce store?

CLV benchmarks by industry

There is no universal good number, because CLV is the product of a category, a price point and a reorder cycle. These ranges are what stores in each vertical typically report, on margin, over the full customer relationship.

IndustryTypical CLVWhy
Fashion and apparel150 to 300 EURSeasonal buying, moderate margin, strong brand pull
Beauty and skincare200 to 400 EURConsumable products, natural reorder cycle
Electronics and accessories300 to 600 EURInfrequent purchases, higher margin per order
Supplements and nutrition400 to 800 EURMonthly consumption, subscription friendly
General dropshipping50 to 150 EURLow frequency, thin margin, weak brand attachment

Use them as a sanity check, not as a target. A 90 EUR CLV is excellent if your acquisition cost is 20 EUR and catastrophic if it is 100 EUR. The absolute number means nothing until you put it next to what you pay to get the customer.

CLV:CAC ratio: the key metric to watch

Three to one is the threshold everyone quotes, and for once the consensus is right: roughly a third of the value goes to fixed costs, logistics and things going wrong. What matters is knowing what to do at each level.

CLV:CAC ratioWhat it meansWhat to do
Above 5:1You are leaving growth on the tableRaise bids, widen audiences, test new channels
3:1 to 5:1Healthy and scalablePush volume, protect retention
1.5:1 to 3:1Viable but tightWork on average order value and repeat rate first
Below 1.5:1UnsustainablePause scaling, fix the offer or the product mix
Below 1:1CriticalEvery new sale deepens the loss, stop the spend

If your ratio is below 1.5:1, you are losing money on every customer you buy. Pause the scaling, fix the offer, the margin or the product mix, and only then turn the spend back on. To keep an eye on the cost side day to day, pair this page with the BEROAS calculator, which gives the break-even ROAS your ads have to beat rather than the value of the customer behind them.

Payback: the constraint a good CLV can hide

A lifetime value spread over four years does not pay this month's invoices. Payback divides your acquisition cost by the monthly margin a customer produces, and it answers a different question: not whether the customer is worth it, but whether you can afford to wait.

A store that recovers its acquisition cost in three months can reinvest the same euro four times a year. A store that takes eighteen months funds its growth out of working capital, and grows exactly as fast as its bank balance allows. Two stores with an identical 4:1 ratio can therefore scale at completely different speeds.

Read the two together. The ratio tells you whether to spend, payback tells you how fast you can spend it again. If payback runs past twelve months, front-load the relationship: a starter bundle, a subscription, or a second-order offer that pulls margin forward instead of waiting for it.

How to increase your customer lifetime value

Four levers move lifetime value, and they are not equal. Average order value and frequency act on the base, churn acts on the multiplier, and the product catalogue sets the ceiling for all three. Work them in that order of effort, but never forget that the fourth one caps the first three.

One warning before optimising: run the calculation on your best cohort as well as your average. On most stores the top fifth of customers carries more than half the profit, and a retention programme aimed at the average customer spends most of its budget on people who were never going to come back.

Increase average order value

The fastest lever, because it needs no new customer. Bundles, upsells at checkout and a free shipping threshold set just above your current average order value all move it within a week.

The compounding matters: a 10 EUR gain in average order value, at 4 orders a year over 3 years, adds 120 EUR of revenue per customer before anything else changes. Subscriptions push it further by turning one purchase into a scheduled one. If you are evaluating that route on Shopify, the Shopify subscription calculator shows what the plan and its fees actually cost you at your volume.

Increase purchase frequency

Frequency is where email and retention flows earn their keep: a post-purchase sequence, a replenishment reminder timed to when the product runs out, a loyalty programme that makes the second order cheaper than the first.

The arithmetic is blunt. Moving from 2 to 3 orders a year raises CLV by 50%, with no change to your margin, your price or your ad spend. That is a bigger swing than most stores get from a full creative overhaul.

Reduce churn

Churn is the variable that moves CLV the hardest, because it acts on the multiplier rather than the base. Cutting annual churn from 40% to 30% takes the average lifespan from 2.5 to 3.3 years, roughly a third more value per customer.

What moves it is unglamorous: an unboxing that looks like the product page promised, delivery estimates that hold, a support reply the same day, a win-back offer sent before the customer forgets you rather than six months after. None of it is a growth hack, all of it is measurable in the retention field above.

Start with products that attract repeat buyers

Everything above assumes your catalogue can be bought twice. Plenty cannot. Furniture, decoration and most electronics are replaced on a cycle measured in years, so no email flow will ever make them a high frequency purchase.

Products with a natural reorder cycle behave differently: skincare, supplements, coffee, pet food, anything consumed or worn out. The second purchase is built into the product instead of being extracted from the customer, and it is the single decision that raises your CLV ceiling before any optimisation.

That is why product selection is a lifetime value decision, not just a margin decision. Copyfy's winning products database analyses over 100,000 products with verified sales data, so you can pick the ones that get reordered instead of discovering the problem three months into an ad budget.

Rich text area:
What is ecommerce ROI?

Return on investment is the share of money that comes back on top of what you put in. In ecommerce it compares what a period actually left in your pocket with what that period cost you: products, advertising, platform fees, shipping and every operating line in between. One percentage, answering the only question that matters at the end of a month: was the money that went in worth the money that came out?

Revenue never answers it. A store can double its revenue and end the month poorer than the last one, because the extra volume was bought with advertising that cost more than the margin it produced. Revenue measures activity, ROI measures whether that activity deserved to run.

ROI vs ROAS: what's the difference?

ROAS divides revenue by ad spend. It is a useful number, but it only judges the advertising, and it treats the product as if it were free. ROI divides net profit by every cost you carry, so it judges the business behind the campaign.

 ROASROI
What it measuresAdvertising onlyThe whole operation
FormulaRevenue / ad spend(Revenue − total costs) / total costs
Includes product cost❌✅
Includes fees and shipping❌✅
Reads asA multiplier, 3.2 for instanceA percentage, 32% for instance
AnswersAre my ads pulling their weight?Am I making money?

Take a store at a 3:1 ROAS, the number most dropshippers treat as the safety line. Revenue of 30,000 on 10,000 of ads looks excellent, until you add 12,000 of product cost, 3,000 of shipping, 1,200 of payment and platform fees and 5,000 of operating costs. Total costs land at 31,200, the store is 1,200 in the red, and the ads manager still shows a green 3:1. If you only ever look at advertising, our ROAS calculator does that one job. ROI is the number that catches the rest.

Why ROI matters more than revenue for dropshippers

Dropshipping runs on thin margins and rented traffic. The product cost moves when the supplier changes, the ad cost moves when the auction heats up, and both movements are invisible in a revenue chart. A store that scales a product on revenue alone is scaling whatever the market gives it, including the losses.

ROI turns that fog into a decision. It tells you the point where extra spend stops adding profit, it tells you which product deserves the next budget increase, and it exposes the ones that only look alive because they sell a lot. Scaling a negative ROI simply loses money faster, and it does it with the exact discipline you were proud of.

How to calculate ecommerce ROI: the formula

The basic ROI formula

The short version fits on one line, and every other formula on this page is a variation of it:

ROI = ((revenue − total costs) / total costs) × 100

The subtraction gives you net profit. The division puts that profit back in proportion to the money it took to produce, which is what makes ROI comparable between a product you sell ten times and one you sell a thousand times.

The full ecommerce ROI formula

The trap is never the formula, it is the cost list. Anything you forget inflates the result, and the missing line is usually the one that quietly kills the month. A complete ecommerce cost base looks like this:

  • Cost of goods sold, supplier shipping included
  • Ad spend across every channel, agency and creative fees included
  • Platform, payment and transaction fees
  • Shipping and fulfilment paid to the customer's door
  • Returns, refunds and chargebacks
  • Operating costs: apps, subscriptions, freelancers, customer support

Which gives the version the calculator above runs on:

Net profit = revenue − COGS − ad spend − fees − shipping − other costs
ROI = (net profit / total costs) × 100

A worked example, with round numbers so you can follow the arithmetic:

LineAmountComment
Revenue10,000What the period brought in
Cost of goods sold3,50035% of revenue, typical of a sourced product
Ad spend2,500A 4:1 ROAS
Platform and payment fees400Subscription plus processing
Shipping500Paid to the customer
Other costs100Apps and tools
Total costs7,000The denominator of the ROI
Net profit3,000Revenue minus total costs
ROI42.9%3,000 / 7,000 × 100

Same store, one change: the supplier raises the product cost by 15% and COGS moves to 4,025. Net profit drops to 2,475 and ROI falls to 32.9%. The revenue line has not moved by a single unit. That gap between an unchanged top line and a collapsing return is exactly what a ROI calculation is for.

The same formula in a spreadsheet

If you would rather track it month after month, six input columns and four formulas rebuild the calculator in any spreadsheet:

ColumnContentFormula
A to FRevenue, COGS, ad spend, fees, shipping, other costsTyped in
GTotal costs=SUM(B2:F2)
HGross profit=A2-B2
INet profit=A2-G2
JROI %=(I2/G2)*100
KROAS=IF(C2=0,"",A2/C2)
LProfit margin %=(I2/A2)*100

One row per month, and the ROI column becomes a trend rather than a snapshot. That is the version worth keeping, because a single month tells you very little and twelve of them tell you where the business is going.

How to use this ecommerce ROI calculator

The calculator sits at the top of this page and runs in two modes. Period mode takes the totals of a month, a quarter or a campaign. Order mode takes the unit economics of a single product and multiplies them by your volume. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the numbers stay in your browser.

Step 1: enter your revenue

In Shopify, open Analytics, then Reports, then Total sales, and pick the period you want to judge. Take the figure net of discounts and refunds, since that is the money that actually reached you. If you sell on several channels, add them up and keep the same perimeter for the costs, otherwise the two sides of the ratio stop describing the same business.

Step 2: enter your costs

Cost of goods comes from the cost per item field on each variant, or straight from your supplier invoices, supplier shipping included. Platform and payment fees are in your Shopify billing page plus your processor statement. Shipping is what you paid to deliver, not what the customer paid you. Other costs is the line most people leave empty and should not: apps, subscriptions, freelancers, support tools, everything you pay to keep the store running.

Step 3: add your ad spend

Pull the amount spent over the same period from your ads manager, across every channel. The field is optional: leave it at zero and you get the ROI of an unadvertised store, which is a fair way to see what your organic sales really carry. Fill it in and the calculator also returns your ROAS, so you can read both numbers side by side instead of choosing between them.

Reading your results

The large percentage is your ROI, with a badge that places it on a scale: a loss below zero, low up to 15%, healthy up to 40%, excellent beyond. Underneath, four cards break the result down.

  • Gross profit: what the sale leaves once the product is paid for
  • Net profit: what remains once everything else is paid too
  • ROAS: your revenue per unit of ad spend, when there is ad spend
  • Profit margin: net profit as a share of revenue

The line below shows your break-even, in revenue for period mode and in orders for order mode, with the distance you still have to cover or the cushion you already have. The interpretation box turns the whole thing into a sentence, including the maximum you can pay to acquire an order before the margin stops absorbing it. If you want to go further into per-order economics, the dropshipping profit margin calculator works the same cost base at the unit level.

What is a good ROI for an ecommerce store?

There is no single good number, because ROI depends on what you had to buy to get the sale. A channel where traffic is rented and priced at auction cannot return what a channel you own returns. The useful comparison is not with another store, it is with your own previous period and with the other channels you run.

ROI benchmarks by channel

There is no reliable public ROI benchmark per channel, and any table handing you a single figure is guessing: inside one niche the spread is wider than the gap between two channels. What is stable is the mechanism, what each channel makes you pay for and what it gives back.

ChannelWhat drives the returnWhat operators report
Paid socialAuction pricing and creative fatigueCost per purchase climbs as you scale and as the brand ages, so the return erodes unless the offer improves
Google ShoppingBuying intent is already thereBids climb with the price of the product, so high-ticket carries the heaviest acquisition cost
EmailAn audience you already own, near-zero marginal costCommonly credited with 20 to 40% of extra yearly revenue on top of paid traffic
SEOFree traffic with buying intent, compounding over timeCuts the weight of ad spend against revenue, which is what lifts the margin
Influencer and UGCPaid per video, not per saleBought mainly for proof and creative volume, at a cost per video rather than a cost per order

The pattern matters more than any benchmark: the channels you rent return the least, the channels you own return the most, and a store built only on paid social carries the thinnest return of all. Retention is the other half of that picture, and the customer lifetime value calculator tells you what a customer is worth beyond the first order.

Break-even ROI: the floor under everything

A ROI of 0% is not failure, it is the exact point where the business pays for itself and nothing more. Everything below is money you are handing over to sell. In period mode the calculator shows that floor as a revenue figure: your total costs. In order mode it shows it as a number of orders, which is the more actionable of the two, because it converts a budget into a target you can act on.

The floor moves with your margin, and this is where most stores misread themselves. On a 20% gross margin, every point of ad cost eats five times more ROI than on a 50% margin. The margin sets the room you have to buy traffic, and no amount of campaign optimisation buys back room the product never had.

How to improve your ecommerce ROI

ROI has a numerator and a denominator, so it moves in two ways: raise what a sale leaves you, or lower what it costs to make that sale happen. In that order, because the first one compounds on every campaign that follows.

Cut your cost of goods

Renegotiate once you have volume to show, ask for the tiered price rather than the list price, and compare two or three suppliers on the same reference before you commit. Bundling your own shipping arrangement instead of paying the supplier's default rate often moves more than a price cut. On a product at 35% margin, taking two points off the cost of goods lifts the ROI more than a full point of extra ROAS.

Raise average order value

The acquisition cost of an order is largely fixed: you paid to bring the customer, not to bring the item. Every extra unit in the same order rides on that cost without adding to it, which is why bundles, volume tiers and a free-shipping threshold set just above your current average move ROI faster than any bid adjustment. A post-purchase upsell is the cleanest version of it, since it adds revenue after the ad has already been paid for.

Stop paying to learn what is already public

A large share of wasted ad spend goes into testing angles that competitors have already validated in public. Their ads are visible, along with how long they have been running, which is the clearest signal a creative is working: nobody keeps paying for an ad that loses money. Reading that before you launch shortens the testing phase, and the testing phase is where ROI goes to die. The Copyfy ads library shows the ads running in your niche, with their duration and their spend, so your budget goes to what already converts.

Pick products that carry margin

The highest-leverage decision happens before the first ad, when you choose what to sell. A product with room between its cost and its market price starts with a better ROI than any campaign can rescue afterwards, and one with two points of margin will never be saved by a clever hook. Sorting on proven demand and on the margin the price allows is what the product research tool is for.

Where to go next

ROI is a snapshot of a period. Two other numbers make it a decision: what a single order really leaves you, and what a customer is worth over time. Both have their own free tool on this site, no account needed, same rule about your data staying in your browser.

How to download a TikTok ad in three steps

The tool works from the TikTok Creative Center, the showcase where TikTok features the best-performing ads on its platform. Everything starts from an ad opened in its Top Ads tab.

  1. Open Creative Center Top Ads, pick a country, an objective and a period, then click the ad you want.
  2. Copy the address of the page that opens. The 19-digit ID it contains works too.
  3. Paste the link into the tool above, run the search and choose the video quality.

Without a TikTok account, the Creative Center only shows a handful of ads per search. A free account unlocks the rest of the ranking, and every ad link works the same way in the tool.

Video links are signed by TikTok and expire after a few hours. If a download fails on an old search, just run the search again to get fresh links.

Why only Creative Center ads?

TikTok publishes its ads in two places, and they do not behave the same way. The Creative Center serves its pages and videos without special restrictions, so the tool can read them the way your browser does. The TikTok Ad Library, the transparency library required in Europe by the Digital Services Act, guards every request with an anti-bot check. The tool does not work around it: an Ad Library link is recognised, and the tool tells you to look for the same ad in the Creative Center.

What to do with a downloaded TikTok ad

An ad that holds its place in Top Ads has already survived the auction. Downloading it lets you watch it frame by frame, where the feed only gives it three seconds of attention:

  • The hook: what happens on screen and what is said before the third second
  • The structure: problem, demonstration, proof, call to action
  • On-screen text and captions, often read more than the voice-over is heard
  • The final call to action and the page it sends people to

File each video with its copy and objective in a folder per product or per angle. After twenty or so ads in the same niche the same hooks keep coming back, and that pattern is what is worth reusing, not the video itself.

An ad remains its advertiser’s property. Download it to study it and learn from it, never to republish it as is in your own campaigns.

Rich text area:
How to download a Facebook ad in three steps

The tool works from the Meta Ad Library, the public database where Meta shows the ads running on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and Threads. You can browse it without an account, and every ad has a unique ID.

  1. Open the Meta Ad Library, pick a country and search for a brand or a keyword.
  2. Open the ad details and copy the page address, which ends with ?id= followed by a number. The library ID shown on the ad card works too.
  3. Paste the link into the tool above, run the search and download the creative you want.

A search link, which contains ?q= or a page name but no ID, doesn’t point to any specific ad: the tool needs the ID of one ad, not a list of results.

What the tool gets for each ad

ItemWhat you get
VideosAn HD MP4 and an SD MP4 when Meta offers both
ImagesThe file at its original size
Carousels and dynamic creativesEach card with its own creative, headline and link, plus a button to download everything
Ad copyThe full primary text, copyable in one click, and the headline
Advertiser and statusThe Facebook page, whether the ad is active or inactive, its start date
PlacementsThe platforms (Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Threads, Audience Network)
Button and landing pageThe call-to-action text and the page the ad sends people to

Creative links are signed by Meta and eventually expire. If a download fails on an old search, just run the search again to get fresh links.

Which ads can you download?

Any ad visible in the Meta Ad Library from its ID: single video, single image, carousel, dynamic creative that rotates several assets, or catalogue ad that shows product cards. Every active ad is visible there. Inactive ads only stay in some cases, including political ads and ads delivered in the European Union.

What you pasteResult
Ad link (…/ads/library/?id=…)✅ Creatives, copy and ad sheet
Library ID only✅ Same result
Ad Library search link❌ No ad ID
Facebook or Instagram post❌ Not supported

Organic posts from pages and Instagram accounts aren’t supported. The tool is built to analyse ads, not to archive accounts.

What to do with a downloaded Facebook ad?

An ad that has been running for several weeks is likely profitable: advertisers quickly cut what doesn’t sell. Downloading it lets you watch it frame by frame, where the feed only gives it a few seconds of attention:

  • The hook: what happens on screen and what is said in the first three seconds
  • The structure: problem, demonstration, proof, call to action
  • The primary text: its length, its angle and the promise of its first line
  • The call-to-action button and the page it sends people to

File each creative with its copy and start date in a folder per product or per angle. After twenty or so ads in the same niche, the same hooks come back, and that pattern is what’s worth reusing, not the video itself.

An ad remains the property of its advertiser. Download it to analyse it and draw inspiration from it, never to republish it as is in your own campaigns.

The Meta Ad Library shows every active ad, but not how it performs: no engagement and no spend for an e-commerce ad. How to analyze a product’s reviews in three steps

Customer reviews are the cheapest market research there is: hundreds of buyers explain why they bought, who for and what let them down. The tool does the sorting for you and turns those reviews into a persona you can actually use.

  1. Open a product page on AliExpress, Amazon or a Shopify store.
  2. Copy the full page URL. Short links like amzn.to aren’t read, so open them first.
  3. Paste the link into the tool above and run the analysis.

The more reviews a product has, the more reliable the profile. On a product with ten reviews, treat the trends as leads, not as certainties.

When you’re not signed in, Amazon only shows a sample of reviews: the analysis then relies on that sample and on the aspects Amazon calculates across all reviews. On Shopify, a store without a review app, or with an unsupported one, returns nothing usable.

What to do with the persona?

A persona drawn from reviews helps you write the way your customers talk. Three uses come up most:

  • Your ads: one angle per strong motivation, with the customers’ exact words in the hook
  • Your product page: a clear answer to each pain point and unmet expectation, in the description or the FAQ
  • Your targeting: countries, people mentioned and usage contexts give you audience ideas to test

Run the analysis on several competitors selling the same product. When the same frustration shows up everywhere, that’s your differentiation angle: fixing it on your page puts you ahead of them.

Rich text area:
How to calculate your CPA in three steps

CPA, or cost per acquisition, is what you pay in advertising to get one purchase. On its own, it says very little: a €25 CPA is excellent on a €120 order and ruinous on a €30 order. That is why the calculator measures it against your own break-even point.

  1. Enter your ad spend and your number of purchases for the same period, plus your clicks if you have them.
  2. Enter your average order value, your product cost, your shipping per order and your payment fees.
  3. Add a target net margin if you want a tougher goal than break-even.

Pull the numbers from your ads manager and your store for the same window, for example the last seven days. Mixing two periods skews the whole calculation.

The formulas used

MetricFormula
CPAAd spend / number of purchases
Break-even CPAAverage order value − product cost − shipping − payment fees
Target CPABreak-even CPA − target net margin × average order value
Profit per orderBreak-even CPA − actual CPA
ROASAverage order value / CPA
BEROASAverage order value / break-even CPA
Maximum CPCGoal CPA × conversion rate
Minimum conversion rateCPC / goal CPA

The calculation covers the first order only. If your customers buy again, they are worth more than their first order and you can accept a higher CPA: that is what the customer lifetime value calculator is for.

A worked example

A store sells a product for €50. It costs the store €15, shipping costs €5 and payment fees take 3% of the order, or €1.50. That leaves €28.50 before advertising: this is its break-even CPA.

ScenarioResult
€1,000 spent for 40 purchasesA €25 CPA, which means €3.50 profit per order and €140 across the campaign
Target net margin of 15%A €21 target CPA: the campaign is profitable but below the goal
2,000 clicks, so a €0.50 CPC and a 2% conversion rateTo hold €21: a CPC of €0.42 at most, or a conversion rate of 2.38% at least

The same campaign with 30 purchases gives a CPA of €33.33: above the threshold, each sale then costs the store €4.83. A few fewer sales are enough to push you into the red.

What is a good CPA?

There is no universal good CPA. A good CPA is one below your break-even CPA, with enough room to cover your fixed costs. Three benchmarks are enough:

  • Above your break-even CPA, every sale costs you money: cut or fix before raising the budget
  • Between your target CPA and break-even, you are profitable but tight: improve conversion before you scale
  • Below your target CPA, you have room: raise the budget step by step while watching your CPA

The same logic works with ROAS. If you manage your campaigns by ROAS, our BEROAS calculator gives you the minimum ROAS to hold directly, and the guide to break-even ROAS breaks down the formula.

How to lower your CPA

Your CPA depends on two things: what a click costs you and the share of clicks that buy. Each lever acts on one of the two, or raises your threshold:

  • Creatives and targeting lower your CPC: an ad that hooks people attracts cheaper clicks
  • The product page raises your conversion rate: social proof, answers to objections, page speed
  • Average order value raises your break-even CPA: bundles, upsells and free shipping above a threshold

For the product page, the Shopify CRO guide brings together the optimizations that win conversion points. On the campaign side, the Facebook Ads dropshipping guide covers structure and creative testing. And once your CPA is below target, the method to scale your Meta Ads campaigns helps you raise the budget without blowing up your CPA.
